content: The Cartesian coordinate system, also known as the rectangular coordinate system, is a mathematical framework used to uniquely identify points in a plane using two numerical values. These values are typically referred to as the x-coordinate (or abscissa) and the y-coordinate (or ordinate). To establish this system, two perpendicular axes, the x-axis and the y-axis, are defined, along with a unit length marked on each axis. This system can also be extended to three-dimensional space, where a third axis, the z-axis, is introduced, or even to higher dimensions. In the Cartesian system, geometric shapes such as curves can be represented algebraically through equations that the coordinates of points on the shape satisfy. For instance, a circle with a radius of 2 can be described by the equation (x^2 + y^2 = 4). The term Cartesian originates from the French mathematician and philosopher René Descartes (Latinized as Cartesius), who played a pivotal role in merging algebra with Euclidean geometry. His work laid the foundation for analytic geometry, calculus, and cartography. Descartes introduced the concept of specifying a point's position on a surface using two intersecting axes in his 1637 writings, particularly in Discourse on Method and La Géométrie. In two dimensions, the Cartesian coordinate system is defined by two perpendicular axes, forming a plane called the xy-plane. The horizontal axis is labeled x, and the vertical axis is labeled y. In three dimensions, an additional axis, the z-axis, is added, providing a third spatial dimension. The axes are typically orthogonal (at right angles to each other), although earlier systems sometimes used oblique axes. The intersection of the axes is called the origin, labeled O. Points in the system are specified as ordered pairs (x, y) in two dimensions or triplets (x, y, z) in three dimensions. The xy-plane is divided into four quadrants by the xand y-axes. These quadrants are labeled counterclockwise using Roman numerals: I (+, +), II (−, +), III (−, −), and IV (+, −). In three dimensions, the space is divided into eight regions called octants by the xy-, yz-, and xz-planes. The first octant contains points where all coordinates (x, y, z) are positive. Orientation in the Cartesian system is determined by the choice of positive and negative directions for the axes. In two dimensions, the standard orientation is right-handed, where the positive x-axis points right, and the positive y-axis points up. This orientation can be visualized using the right-hand rule: placing the right hand on the plane with the thumb pointing up, the fingers curl from the x-axis to the y-axis. Reversing the roles of the xand y-axes changes the orientation. In three dimensions, the right-hand rule also applies, with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger representing the x-, y-, and z-axes, respectively. A left-handed system can be defined similarly using the left hand. The Cartesian coordinate system is foundational in representing vectors. A point in space can be represented as a vector originating from the origin and pointing to the point. In three dimensions, this vector can be expressed as (mathbf{r} = xmathbf{i} + ymathbf{j} + zmathbf{k}), where (mathbf{i}), (mathbf{j}), and (mathbf{k}) are unit vectors along the x-, y-, and z-axes, respectively. These unit vectors form the standard basis in three-dimensional space. Cartesian coordinates are widely used to represent spatial dimensions but can also represent other quantities such as mass, time, or force. In such cases, the axes may be labeled with different letters (e.g., m, t, F) and may have different units of measurement. The system can be extended to higher dimensions to represent relationships between more than three variables, even though such spaces are difficult to visualize. The algebra of Cartesian coordinates, however, can be extended to handle these higher dimensions, enabling complex calculations. In computational geometry, the Cartesian coordinate system serves as the foundation for algebraic manipulation of geometric shapes. Other coordinate systems, such as polar coordinates or spherical coordinates, have been developed for specific applications. For example, astronomers and physicists often use spherical coordinates to describe three-dimensional space. It is speculated that Renaissance artists' use of grids to break down their subjects may have influenced Descartes' development of the Cartesian system, though this remains speculative.
